qAndA.answer: Dextrin helps to stabilize the silver chloride precipitate, preventing it from coagulating and making the endpoint color change easier to see.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of adding dextrin to the solution?

qAndA.answer: Adding the indicator too early can lead to photoreduction of the silver ions, forming black particles that obscure the desired pink color change at the endpoint.
qAndA.question: Why is it crucial to add the indicator near the endpoint and not at the beginning?

qAndA.answer: A very light pink color, not a dark pink. This indicates that all the chloride has been precipitated.
qAndA.question: What color change should you look for at the endpoint of the titration?

qAndA.answer: The color of the solution can change over time due to photoreduction, so comparisons to earlier titrations might not be accurate.
qAndA.question: Why should you avoid comparing the endpoint color to previous titrations?

qAndA.answer: Dichlorofluorescein. It turns pink when adsorbed onto silver chloride particles in the absence of excess chloride.
qAndA.question: What is the indicator used in this titration?

reaction.
In this titration, it is crucial to add dextrine to each flask.
The dextrine can be pre-weight, only weighing about 0.1 grams, and kept in waypapers until
ready to be added to each flask.
It can be added well in advance of the titration.
And no, I did not throw the white paper on the floor.
There is, in fact, a garbage on the other side of the desk.
After the dextrine has been added to the solution, add additional water to break it up,
and ensure that as much of it is dissolved as possible.
You can rinse down the sides with the ionized water.
The indicator using this titration is dichloroforesine.
The indicator can absorb onto the surface of the silver chloride particles, but only
when there is no excess chloride present in solution.
When all the chloride has been precipitated by the addition of silver, the florescene
will then add absorb onto those particles, going from a yellow color to a pink end point
color.
Your first titration will be a rough titration, where you add the florescene right away.
You will then rapidly add titrant to reach the end point, or at least a rough approximation.
And the reason for this is that the addition of florescene to the titration flask is detrimental
to the proper visualization of the end point.
The florescene accelerates the photo reduction of the silver ions, leading to the formation
of black particles.
These black particles make it difficult to visualize the color change from yellow to pink.
For future titrations, you will not add the florescene indicator until you are a couple
of milliliters away from this rough end point.
All other aspects of the titration are the same.
You will add the dextram before doing the titration, you will rinse it down with some
dey water, and you will carefully record the volume on the burette before beginning
your titration.
Since a rough end point is already known for this titration, you can add titrant rapidly
until you are a couple of milliliters from that end point volume.
Do remember to swirl and occasionally rinse down the sides of your flask.
It is so important to maintain proper analytical technique, even though you are going rapidly.
Once you are within a few milliliters of the approximate end point, you will want to
add the dichloroforecene indicator solution.
You only need about four or five drops in order to be able to see the color very nicely
in this solution.
Now proceed to slowly and carefully add titrant until you begin noticing a pink color up

As with other titrations, the longer this end point color persists, the closer you are
to the end point.
Continue to swirl the flask and rinse down the sides periodically to ensure that all reagents

youtube_description: This video demonstrates the precipitation titration of chloride using silver nitrate and dichlorofluorescein as an indicator, a process otherwise known as Fajan's method.
